implementation_notes: No framework is required: read the selection with URLSearchParams, keep a per-resource allowlist, and build the reply with Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(row).filter(([k]) => keep.has(k))). Nested selections recurse with the same helper. This is the whole classic structure - mask parsing, validation and the projection - collapsed into a few lines, which is why the pattern is idiomatic here rather than a class hierarchy; GraphQL remains the library-backed alternative.
pitfalls: Request keys must be checked against the allowlist before they are used at all - never spread or assign caller-supplied keys into a response object (__proto__-style keys and prototype pollution).
JSON.stringify drops undefined values silently, so a field that was selected but is missing looks exactly like a field that was never selected; decide null versus omit explicitly.

The projection copies the row: on large collections prefer a pre-built serializer per view, and keep an explicit Vary/ETag strategy because the same URL with different selectors yields different bytes.

variants.name: GraphQL execution with selection-set-aware resolvers
variants.idiom_name: GraphQL field resolvers receive the selection set (info.fieldNodes) and only selected fields run
variants.implementation_notes: With a GraphQL layer the selection set is the request: the executor calls a field's resolver only when the client selected it, so the projection is structural rather than a filter applied to a finished payload. Fields whose cost is not obvious (nested lists, remote calls) still inspect the selection - info.fieldNodes via a helper such as graphql-js's field-node utilities - before doing expensive work.
pitfalls: A selection set is not an authorization mechanism: field-level permissions must be enforced in the resolver, otherwise a client simply names the field it should not see.
Lazy per-field loading turns into N+1 queries unless nested resolvers are batched (DataLoader); the partial response arrives, but the boundary stops being cheap.
Selection-dependent resolver behaviour makes caching harder: the same object id produces different work per document, so cache keys must include the operation (persisted queries / APQ help).
